reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / movement disorder literature
clinicalPearls: Episodic involuntary trembling of the chin and lower lip, caused by contraction of the mentalis muscle
It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and usually begins in early childhood
Episodes are typically triggered by emotion, stress or concentration and last seconds to minutes
The movements can occasionally be intense enough to interfere with speech or, rarely, disrupt sleep
It is benign, and diagnosis is clinical, supported by a positive family history
Treatment is often unnecessary, though botulinum toxin to the mentalis muscle helps troublesome cases
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary geniospasm is a benign familial movement disorder in which involuntary rhythmic or trembling contractions of the mentalis muscle produce chin and lower-lip quivering. It is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with linkage reported to a locus on chromosome 9, and the movements are thought to reflect a central hyperexcitability affecting the facial motor control for the chin, provoked by emotional and cognitive arousal. The disorder is not associated with progressive neurological disease.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic chin trembling and family history
Examination localising the movement to the mentalis muscle
Exclusion of tics and dystonia on clinical grounds
Genetic counselling where a family history is present
Further investigation only if atypical features suggest another disorder
redFlags: Onset in adulthood without family history
Spread beyond the chin or additional neurological signs
Features suggesting a tic disorder or dystonia needing separate management
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and lifelong, tending to lessen with age; it does not shorten life or herald other neurological disease, and troublesome cases respond to botulinum toxin.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for a tic or facial dystonia
Overlooking the autosomal dominant family history
Investigating a clearly benign familial condition excessively
Failing to offer botulinum toxin when episodes are socially disabling
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Reassurance about the benign, lifelong nature of the condition, since treatment is often unnecessary and symptoms tend to lessen with age
Botulinum toxin injection into the mentalis muscle for socially or functionally troublesome chin and lip quivering
Trial of an anticonvulsant or benzodiazepine reported to help severe episodes that disrupt speech or sleep
Advice on recognising and moderating emotional stress and concentration as provoking triggers
Genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant inheritance, supported by a positive family history
Reassess if atypical or progressive features emerge, to exclude tics, dystonia or other movement disorders
